title: Gifts of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12)
hookLine: wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, tongues: one Spirit, many gifts, one body

cards: A letter is being read aloud to a church in Corinth, and the room is tense. Paul has heard things. Some there have spectacular gifts and seem to know it.

Others feel they bring nothing. So Paul writes a strange, mixed list: a word of wisdom, a word of knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, telling spirits apart, tongues, and the interpreting of tongues.
Some sound quiet and some sound loud. And like a drumbeat he repeats one phrase: by the same Spirit. To one this, by the same Spirit.
To another that. In this list he isn't ranking anyone. He's tying the whole room together.

teach.h: A GIFT FOR SOMEONE ELSE'S GOOD.
teach.b: Charism is the church's word for a gift of the Spirit: given not as a prize, but for someone else's good. Day two hundred ninety-five met the Pentecostal side of these gifts; today, Paul's chapter itself.

teach.h: DIVERSITIES OF GIFTS, THE SAME SPIRIT.
teach.b: It opens, in the King James: "Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit." And why they're given: "the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal." For the common good.
A gift that only makes its owner look impressive has missed the point. Then Paul reaches for a body. A foot might say, I'm not a hand, so I'm not part of this.
An ear might say, I'm not an eye. If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be?

teach.h: THE EYE CAN'T SAY: NO NEED OF THEE.
teach.b: Then the line that turns the room around: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee."
The parts that "seem to be more feeble, are necessary." Not tolerated. Necessary.
Christians read this chapter differently. Pentecostal and charismatic churches give great weight to the gifts that show, like healing, prophecy and tongues, and expect them in worship today.
Catholic teaching uses charism broadly, for gifts as quiet as teaching or care for the sick, and speaks of whole religious orders having their own charism.
Other churches stress gifts like leading, giving and encouraging, which Paul names in Romans.
Underneath sits Paul's picture: many gifts, one Spirit, one body. And notice what comes right after this chapter. It's the one about love.

how: Christians read 1 Corinthians 12 as teaching that each member of the church has gifts for the good of all; Pentecostal and charismatic churches expect gifts like healing, prophecy and tongues in worship, and Catholic teaching speaks of many kinds of charisms, including those of religious orders.

s: in the list of gifts in 1 Corinthians 12:8–10, Paul ranks them greatest to least

that list keeps repeating "by the same Spirit." later in the chapter (12:28) he does set apostles, prophets and teachers first, second and third, but he also says the weaker-seeming parts are necessary.
Paul says the gifts are given for the common good
"the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal."
Catholic teaching uses the word charism only for miracles
it uses charism broadly, for quiet gifts like teaching too, and for the gift of whole religious orders.

games.q: you're Paul. some in Corinth flaunt their gifts; others feel they bring nothing. how do you answer?
o: tell the gifted ones to stop using their gifts.
tell the quiet ones their gifts don't count.
say every gift comes from one Spirit, for one body.
games.why: he answers with a body: the eye can't say to the hand "I have no need of thee," and the feeble-seeming parts are necessary.

practice: Bring to mind one person, at church, at work or at home, and skip their obvious talents; look for the quiet gift, like noticing who's left out, or calming a room.
Give that gift a name in a few plain words, and sit with the thought that the people around them need it. If you pray, give thanks for that person by name; if you don't, just hold their gift in mind.

wordCard.voice: Charism. A gift of the Spirit, given for the good of others, one of many in one body.

orig.note: Greek: a gift freely given — Paul's word for the Spirit's gifts in 1 Corinthians 12.
